title: Release an uncontrollable outcome while taking your next step

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: Releasing an outcome means acknowledging another person’s control while carrying out one’s own responsibilities. It is compatible with one useful clarification; it does not require extinguishing an urge or feeling.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: Jo invites Rae to a free accessible reading room Saturday 14:00–15:00. The room is confirmed open and suitable; either can attend alone. Jo asks for a reply by Friday 18:00 and says declining is welcome. At Friday 16:00 no reply exists. Jo’s available alternative is reading an already borrowed book at home. Neither has travel or care duties depending on Rae’s answer.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Write one bounded decision rule and distinguish what Jo can choose from what remains Rae’s decision. Save it before the supplied outcome.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: A weather cancellation arrives before an agreed decision time. Must someone ignore it to prove surrender?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: Wait until the stated point without repeated pressure, then choose the feasible alternative if no response. Later fiction: no answer by 18:00; Jo reads at home Saturday and still feels disappointed. Rae’s motive is unknown. Partial: plan a fallback without a decision point. Incorrect: infer rejection, send repeated demands or report a shared visit. Actual control-release behavior would need a real opportunity.
criteria: The fallback and decision time are feasible
Uncertainty and feeling are not rewritten as certainty

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: No. Respond to useful new information and adjust the plan. Releasing control is not neglecting an available responsible action.
criteria: The fallback and decision time are feasible
Uncertainty and feeling are not rewritten as certainty
